comments.author: @ephimp3189
comments.text: As a software engineer, I am still waiting for AI that can actually design things properly. It always seems confident about its solutions, but the designs are often terrible, it basically creates massive tech debt right from the start. So while you may "one shot" some stupid game from scratch, most likely the core design is so bad you can't really build on top of it. AI is still great for working on smaller problems within your established framework, but asking it to make something new is almost always a terrible idea. It's a bit annoying to see people "test" these models by asking them to do some task from scratch, looking only at end result and not bother evaluating the core design decisions of the code itself.

comments.author: @desmond-hawkins
comments.text: (8:33) It's true that "vibe coding" lets lots of people build apps, but using AI coding assistants when you're learning a language or framework or library can certainly be detrimental. There was an MIT paper recently ("Your Brain on ChatGPT: …") that showed students that got help from an LLM while writing an essay remembered a lot less of it, were less capable of summarizing the topic and arguments, etc. compared to students with no AI help. Essentially, they didn't really learn, they outsourced this brain activity to a machine, and therefore did not benefit from the exercise like students that did not get help from AI. Out of 3 groups from no AI to full writing help: the more help they got, the less they acquired this knowledge and these skills. It will be the same for any junior dev who has graduated but still has a lot to learn. I don't envy them.

comments.text:
Anywhere from 60%-80% of most tech companies' expenses are labour related. In a market where interest rates are high and growth is slow, how do you grow revenue? By slashing costs.
It isn't about increasing productivity, increasing productivity doesn't matter if the market is already saturated, it's about increasing profit margins through reduced costs. Why employ 5 engineers when you can get the same bang for your buck by employing 1 engineer and an AI software engineering subscription?
Even if AI reduces headcount by only 10%, that's a savings of potentially hundreds of millions for a tech company. If say, Microsoft, fired 10,000 low-mid level engineers that were earning ~$80,000 per year, that's a savings of $800,000,000. That's not speculation, why do you think there are so many Indians in tech? Because they earn (on average) less than the going market labour rate and this artificially lowers the market rate for skilled labour across the board. This is all about megacorps nickel and dimming us because all those pennies add up

comments.text:
I agree, I don't think AI coding models are going to be putting developers out of work... until maybe we get sentient AI at least. All it's going to do is increase companies expectations on how much work you do in a given amount of time. It will also increase the demand for bespoke software solutions that were previously not financially viable, but thanks to the speed and ease of AI coding, they are quite affordable.
We may see a downsizing of companies as some stupid CEO's are willing to trade long-term market position for short-term gains - we're already seeing this with Salesforce, Microsoft, Google, etc. If I were a shareholder in companies that are laying off due to AI, I'd dump my stock in a hurry. The smarter competition will leverage AI to blow past the industry leaders that took the short-term win and in a couple of years, those industry leaders will be going head-to-head instead, if they aren't flat out playing catchup.
